milestones.title: lint a toolset and count what it costs

functions.name: lint
functions.signature: def lint(tools: List[dict]) -> List[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
functions.doc:
Review tool definitions; return findings as (tool name, code, message).

Codes, in the order they are reported for each tool:
  "thin"            the description has fewer than 15 words
  "restates"        words(description) is a subset of words(name with "_" as spaces)
  then for each property in schema order:
  "generic_arg"     the property name is in GENERIC
  "undescribed_arg" the property has neither a "description" nor an "enum"
After every tool has been reviewed, one more kind of finding:
  "overlap"         for each PAIR of tools (a, b) in list order, the Jaccard similarity of
                    words(a description) and words(b description), |A & B| / |A | B|, is at
                    least 0.35. Report it against tool a; the message names both tools.
Messages are sentences for a human; tests look at the tool name and the code.

functions.name: definition_tokens
functions.doc: Tokens the definitions cost on EVERY request: the sum of count_tokens(json.dumps(tool)).

milestones.task: Write lint(tools), returning findings as (tool name, code, message), and definition_tokens(tools). The five codes (thin, restates, generic_arg, undescribed_arg, overlap), their order and their thresholds are in the docstring; words and GENERIC are given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 1 shows this milestone as ✔. It expects exactly the 13 findings that chapter 5 prints for the thin wrappers, in order, none for the redesign, the edge cases (14 words is thin, 15 is not; a Jaccard of exactly 0.35 counts as overlap; an enum needs no description; overlap comes last), the token counts 217 and 488, and sixty seeded random tools.
hints: len(description.split()) < 15 for thin; words(desc) <= words(name.replace("_", " ")) for restates (<= is the subset test on sets).
The two argument checks run for every property of tool["input_schema"].get("properties", {}): generic_arg if the name is in GENERIC, then undescribed_arg if it has neither "description" nor "enum".
Overlap is the Jaccard similarity of two word sets: len(a & b) / len(a | b). Use itertools.combinations(tools, 2) after the per-tool loop, and report against the first tool of the pair.
Tokens: count_tokens(json.dumps(tool)) per definition, summed. Use the default json.dumps so your count matches the chapter's.
milestones.solution:
def lint(tools: List[dict]) -> List[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
    """Review tool definitions; return findings as (tool name, code, message).

    Codes, in the order they are reported for each tool:
      "thin"            the description has fewer than 15 words
      "restates"        words(description) is a subset of words(name with "_" as spaces)
      then for each property in schema order:
      "generic_arg"     the property name is in GENERIC
      "undescribed_arg" the property has neither a "description" nor an "enum"
    After every tool has been reviewed, one more kind of finding:
      "overlap"         for each PAIR of tools (a, b) in list order, the Jaccard similarity of
                        words(a description) and words(b description), |A & B| / |A | B|, is at
                        least 0.35. Report it against tool a; the message names both tools.
    Messages are sentences for a human; tests look at the tool name and the code.
    """
    out: List[Tuple[str, str, str]] = []
    for t in tools:
        d, n = t["description"], t["name"]
        if len(d.split()) < 15:
            out.append((n, "thin", f"description is {len(d.split())} words; say what, when, when not, and what comes back"))
        if words(d) <= words(n.replace("_", " ")):
            out.append((n, "restates", "description only restates the name"))
        for p, spec in t["input_schema"].get("properties", {}).items():
            if p in GENERIC:
                out.append((n, "generic_arg", f"argument '{p}' has a generic name; prefer customer_id, invoice_id ..."))
            if "description" not in spec and "enum" not in spec:
                out.append((n, "undescribed_arg", f"argument '{p}' has no description"))
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(tools, 2):
        wa, wb = words(a["description"]), words(b["description"])
        j = len(wa & wb) / max(1, len(wa | wb))
        if j >= 0.35:
            out.append((a["name"], "overlap", f"description overlaps {b['name']} by {j:.0%}; a model may confuse them"))
    return out

def definition_tokens(tools: List[dict]) -> int:
    """Tokens the definitions cost on EVERY request: the sum of count_tokens(json.dumps(tool))."""
    return sum(count_tokens(json.dumps(t)) for t in tools)
milestones.explain:
The cheapest measurement needs no runs at all. A linter is a program that reads something and reports likely defects without executing it. Chapter 5 listed the defects a tool definition can have, and most of them can be checked mechanically: a description too short to say what, when, when not and what comes back; a description that only restates the name; generic argument names such as id; arguments with no description; and two tools whose descriptions overlap so much that a model has to guess between them. You write the linter that chapter 5 sketched, and a function that prices a toolset in tokens.

The token count matters because definitions are sent on every request, so their size is a per-call tax. A linter finding is a cheap proxy; it cannot tell you whether the extra words fix real mistakes. That is what the runs are for. Run the solution on both toolsets:

from starter import BETTER, THIN, definition_tokens, lint

for label, tools in (("thin wrappers", THIN), ("task-shaped", BETTER)):
    findings = lint(tools)
    print(f"== {label}: {len(tools)} tools, {definition_tokens(tools)} tokens, {len(findings)} findings")
    for tool, code, message in findings[:4]:
        print(f"   {tool:14s} {code:16s} {message}")
== thin wrappers: 5 tools, 217 tokens, 13 findings
   get_customer   thin             description is 3 words; say what, when, when not, and what comes back
   get_customer   generic_arg      argument 'id' has a generic name; prefer customer_id, invoice_id ...
   get_customer   undescribed_arg  argument 'id' has no description
   list_invoices  thin             description is 2 words; say what, when, when not, and what comes back
== task-shaped: 3 tools, 488 tokens, 0 findings

The 13 findings are the ones chapter 5 prints, and the 271 extra tokens per call (488 against 217) are the price of the redesign. Whether it pays depends on what the extra words prevent, which the rest of the lab measures. Notice the asymmetry as well: a linter can tell you a description is short, but not that it is wrong. A description can pass every rule and still send the model to the wrong tool.
milestones.card:
A linter is a program that reports likely defects in something without running it, and most weaknesses of a tool definition (a thin description, a vague argument name, two tools that overlap) can be found that way. Definitions are also sent on every request, so their size is a per-call cost you can count.

lint(tools) returns (tool name, code, message) tuples with the five codes in the docstring's order, and the overlap findings come last, after every tool has been reviewed. Take the thresholds exactly: fewer than 15 words is thin, so 14 is and 15 is not, and a similarity of exactly 0.35 counts as overlap. Similarity here is the Jaccard measure: the words two descriptions share, divided by all the different words in both. Compare each pair once and report it against the first tool. words and GENERIC are already written, and definition_tokens adds up count_tokens(json.dumps(tool)).

A = {find, customer, email}    B = {find, customer, invoice, owed}
shared 2 of 5 different words = 0.4, at least 0.35: an overlap

functions.name: find_customer
functions.doc:
billing_find_customer: up to 5 matches as [{"customer_id", "name", "email"}, ...].

Use db.match_customers. When nothing matches, RETURN (do not raise) a sentence that
starts "No customer found for" followed by the repr of the text, and tells the model
what to try next (the email address on the account). A name shared by two customers
returns both: it is the model's job to ask which one.

functions.name: account_summary
functions.signature: def account_summary(db: Northwind, customer_id: str, response_format: str = "concise"):
functions.doc:
billing_get_account_summary: one dict that answers "what do they owe / what did they pay".

Raises ToolError(f"No customer with id {customer_id!r}. Ids look like cus_1042; get one from
billing_find_customer.") for an unknown id. Otherwise the dict has exactly these keys:
  customer_id, name, plan
  owed_cents          the sum of amount_cents over ALL invoices with status open or overdue
  open_invoices       the newest 5 of those invoices, newest first, each
                      {"invoice_id", "status", "amount_cents", "due"} (due = the invoice's due_at);
                      with response_format "detailed" each also has "line_items"
  latest_payment      the newest payment as {"payment_id", "invoice_id", "amount_cents", "paid_at"}, or None
  recent_payments     the newest 5 payments, same shape, newest first (latest_payment is the first)
"Newest" payments sort by (paid_at, id) descending, which is what db.payments_of returns.
Invoices come from db.invoices_of (newest first). Nothing else (no addresses, no audit trail).

functions.name: issue_refund
functions.signature: def issue_refund(db: Northwind, payment_id: str, amount_cents: int, reason: str):
functions.doc:
billing_issue_refund: refund part or all of a payment, safely.

1. If amount_cents is above REFUND_CAP_CENTS, raise ToolError whose text contains "human",
   says not to retry, and states the cap. (Enforce it in code, whatever the prompt said.)
2. Otherwise call db.apply_refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=key) with
   key = f"{payment_id}:{amount_cents}:{reason}", so an identical request is never applied twice.
     KeyError          -> ToolError(f"Error: no payment {payment_id!r}. Payment ids look like
                          pay_88123; get one from billing_get_account_summary.")
     ValueError        -> ToolError naming the legal range "between 1 and N" (N = what is still
                          refundable on that payment) and reminding the model amounts are in cents
     RefundTimeout     -> ToolError saying the service timed out and the outcome is unknown, that
                          retrying the SAME call is safe because repeats are ignored
3. On success return f"Refunded {amount_cents} cents of {payment_id} ({reason}); {left} cents still
   refundable." and, when the backend says replayed, append " (repeat of an earlier call: no money moved again)".

Let the backend decide whether the amount is possible (do not pre-check it): after a lost response
the retry must reach the backend with the same key, even if nothing is left to refund.

milestones.task: Write the three functions behind design B: find_customer(db, email_or_name), account_summary(db, customer_id, response_format) and issue_refund(db, payment_id, amount_cents, reason). build_registry("B", db) wires them to the definitions in BETTER, and the stand-in agent calls them. The exact return shapes, error texts and the order of operations are in the docstrings.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 2 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the lookup (email, name, two customers sharing a name, no match), the summary against numbers computed from the raw data for every customer (and that it stays under 450 tokens for the customer whose raw dump is over 10,000), every refund path (success, repeat, wrong reason, out-of-range, unknown payment, over the cap), the lost-response retry, and sixty seeded random refund sequences on a flaky backend: the same payment and amount never moves money twice and nothing ever goes above a payment's total or the cap.
hints: db.match_customers(text) already ignores case and surrounding spaces. Return a string for no match (a result, not an exception) and a list of at most five dicts otherwise.
owed_cents sums all open and overdue invoices; open_invoices lists only the newest five. Do not forget to leave addresses, audit trails and line items out of the concise form.

In issue_refund check the cap first (it needs no database), then call db.apply_refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=key) inside a try. Catch KeyError (unknown payment), ValueError (impossible amount) and RefundTimeout separately; each gets its own message.
Do not compare the amount with what is left before calling the backend. After a lost response nothing is left, and the retry would be refused as out of range instead of being recognised as a repeat.
The tool must say "cents" in its range error and "retry the same call" in its timeout error: those two sentences are what the stand-in agent, like a real model, acts on.
milestones.solution:
def find_customer(db: Northwind, email_or_name: str):
    """billing_find_customer: up to 5 matches as [{"customer_id", "name", "email"}, ...].

    Use db.match_customers. When nothing matches, RETURN (do not raise) a sentence that
    starts "No customer found for" followed by the repr of the text, and tells the model
    what to try next (the email address on the account). A name shared by two customers
    returns both: it is the model's job to ask which one.
    """
    found = db.match_customers(email_or_name)
    if not found:
        return f"No customer found for {email_or_name!r}. Try the email address on the account."
    return [{"customer_id": c["customer_id"], "name": c["name"], "email": c["email"]} for c in found[:5]]

def account_summary(db: Northwind, customer_id: str, response_format: str = "concise"):
    """billing_get_account_summary: one dict that answers "what do they owe / what did they pay".

    Raises ToolError(f"No customer with id {customer_id!r}. Ids look like cus_1042; get one from
    billing_find_customer.") for an unknown id. Otherwise the dict has exactly these keys:
      customer_id, name, plan
      owed_cents          the sum of amount_cents over ALL invoices with status open or overdue
      open_invoices       the newest 5 of those invoices, newest first, each
                          {"invoice_id", "status", "amount_cents", "due"} (due = the invoice's due_at);
                          with response_format "detailed" each also has "line_items"
      latest_payment      the newest payment as {"payment_id", "invoice_id", "amount_cents", "paid_at"}, or None
      recent_payments     the newest 5 payments, same shape, newest first (latest_payment is the first)
    "Newest" payments sort by (paid_at, id) descending, which is what db.payments_of returns.
    Invoices come from db.invoices_of (newest first). Nothing else (no addresses, no audit trail).
    """
    c = db.customers.get(customer_id)
    if c is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No customer with id {customer_id!r}. Ids look like cus_1042; get one from billing_find_customer.")
    open_rows = [i for i in db.invoices_of(customer_id) if i["status"] in ("open", "overdue")]
    pays = [{"payment_id": p["id"], "invoice_id": p["invoice_id"], "amount_cents": p["amount_cents"], "paid_at": p["paid_at"]}
            for p in db.payments_of(customer_id)[:5]]
    listed = []
    for i in open_rows[:5]:
        row = {"invoice_id": i["id"], "status": i["status"], "amount_cents": i["amount_cents"], "due": i["due_at"]}
        if response_format == "detailed":
            row["line_items"] = i["line_items"]
        listed.append(row)
    return {"customer_id": customer_id, "name": c["name"], "plan": c["plan"], "owed_cents": sum(i["amount_cents"] for i in open_rows),
            "open_invoices": listed, "latest_payment": pays[0] if pays else None, "recent_payments": pays}

def issue_refund(db: Northwind, payment_id: str, amount_cents: int, reason: str):
    """billing_issue_refund: refund part or all of a payment, safely.

    1. If amount_cents is above REFUND_CAP_CENTS, raise ToolError whose text contains "human",
       says not to retry, and states the cap. (Enforce it in code, whatever the prompt said.)
    2. Otherwise call db.apply_refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=key) with
       key = f"{payment_id}:{amount_cents}:{reason}", so an identical request is never applied twice.
         KeyError          -> ToolError(f"Error: no payment {payment_id!r}. Payment ids look like
                              pay_88123; get one from billing_get_account_summary.")
         ValueError        -> ToolError naming the legal range "between 1 and N" (N = what is still
                              refundable on that payment) and reminding the model amounts are in cents
         RefundTimeout     -> ToolError saying the service timed out and the outcome is unknown, that
                              retrying the SAME call is safe because repeats are ignored
    3. On success return f"Refunded {amount_cents} cents of {payment_id} ({reason}); {left} cents still
       refundable." and, when the backend says replayed, append " (repeat of an earlier call: no money moved again)".

    Let the backend decide whether the amount is possible (do not pre-check it): after a lost response
    the retry must reach the backend with the same key, even if nothing is left to refund.
    """
    if amount_cents > REFUND_CAP_CENTS:
        raise ToolError(f"Error: refunds above {REFUND_CAP_CENTS} cents need a human. Do not retry. "
                        "Tell the customer a human colleague will review it.")
    key = f"{payment_id}:{amount_cents}:{reason}"
    try:
        res = db.apply_refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=key)
    except KeyError:
        raise ToolError(f"Error: no payment {payment_id!r}. Payment ids look like pay_88123; get one from billing_get_account_summary.")
    except ValueError:
        p = db.payments[payment_id]
        left = p["amount_cents"] - p["refunded_cents"]
        raise ToolError(f"Error: amount_cents must be between 1 and {left} for {payment_id}; got {amount_cents}. Amounts are in cents.")
    except RefundTimeout:
        raise ToolError("The refund service timed out and the outcome is unknown. Retry the same call: "
                        "repeats are ignored, so money cannot move twice.")
    msg = f"Refunded {amount_cents} cents of {payment_id} ({reason}); {res['remaining_cents']} cents still refundable."
    return msg + (" (repeat of an earlier call: no money moved again)" if res["replayed"] else "")
milestones.explain:
Design A is what you get by wrapping a REST API one endpoint at a time: easy to build, complete on paper, and designed for a different user, a programmer who already holds a customer id and is happy to join four resources. A model holds an email address and nothing else. Design B starts from the tasks instead. Four moves from chapter 5 turn into code in this milestone:

  • Make the first step reachable. find_customer accepts the thing the user actually gave you (an email or a name) and returns candidate ids. When two customers share a name it returns both, because choosing between them is the model's job (and, in tasks 19 and 20, the right behaviour is to ask).
  • Send back what the next step needs. account_summary joins customer, open invoices and recent payments server-side and returns a small dictionary. For the customer with 60 invoices that is a few hundred tokens instead of more than ten thousand, and it includes the payment_id the refund tool needs.
  • Make errors teach. An unknown payment says what ids look like and where to get one; an impossible amount says the legal range and the unit; a refund above the cap says so, says a human decides, and says not to retry.
  • Enforce safety in code. The cap is a line of Python, not a sentence in the description, and the refund carries an idempotency key.

The last move deserves its own paragraph, because it is subtle and because it is the same mechanism as in failure, timeouts and retries. The backend's refund service in this lab is flaky in a realistic way: it applies the refund and then the response is lost, so the caller sees a timeout and does not know whether money moved. A caller that retries blindly refunds twice. An idempotency key is a caller-chosen token sent with a write so that repeating the same request has the effect of sending it once: the backend remembers the key and returns the first result. Your tool derives the key from the request itself (payment_id:amount:reason), so the model needs no new argument and the retry is recognised.

import json
from fixtures import Northwind
from llm import count_tokens
from standin import ToolError
from starter import account_summary, find_customer, issue_refund

db = Northwind()
print(find_customer(db, "Ana Silva"))
print(find_customer(db, "nobody@example.com"))
raw = json.dumps(db.invoices_of("cus_1042"))
summary = account_summary(db, "cus_1042")
print(f"\nraw invoice dump: {count_tokens(raw):,} tokens;  summary: {count_tokens(json.dumps(summary))} tokens")
print(json.dumps({k: summary[k] for k in ("name", "owed_cents", "latest_payment")}))
print(f"open invoices: {[(i['invoice_id'], i['status'], i['amount_cents']) for i in summary['open_invoices']]}")

print("\n-- a refund whose response is lost --")
flaky = Northwind(flaky=True)
for attempt in (1, 2):
    try:
        print(attempt, issue_refund(flaky, "pay_88124", 4900, "duplicate"))
    except ToolError as e:
        print(attempt, "ToolError:", e)
print("money moved:", flaky.refunds)
for amount in (25000, 99999):
    try:
        issue_refund(Northwind(), "pay_88450", amount, "goodwill")
    except ToolError as e:
        print(f"{amount}: {e}")
[{'customer_id': 'cus_1042', 'name': 'Ana Silva', 'email': 'ana@example.com'}, {'customer_id': 'cus_1046', 'name': 'Ana Silva', 'email': 'ana.silva@work.example'}]
No customer found for 'nobody@example.com'. Try the email address on the account.

raw invoice dump: 10,874 tokens;  summary: 235 tokens
{"name": "Ana Silva", "owed_cents": 9800, "latest_payment": {"payment_id": "pay_88124", "invoice_id": "inv_3001", "amount_cents": 4900, "paid_at": "2026-03-05"}}
open invoices: [('inv_3000', 'open', 4900), ('inv_3002', 'overdue', 4900)]

-- a refund whose response is lost --
1 ToolError: The refund service timed out and the outcome is unknown. Retry the same call: repeats are ignored, so money cannot move twice.
2 Refunded 4900 cents of pay_88124 (duplicate); 0 cents still refundable. (repeat of an earlier call: no money moved again)
money moved: [('pay_88124', 4900)]
25000: Error: refunds above 10000 cents need a human. Do not retry. Tell the customer a human colleague will review it.
99999: Error: refunds above 10000 cents need a human. Do not retry. Tell the customer a human colleague will review it.

Read the last block carefully. The first attempt raised a timeout error, but money moved shows one refund. The second attempt returned a normal message saying nothing moved again, and still shows one refund. Notice the message after the retry: 0 cents still refundable. If your tool had checked the amount against the remaining balance before calling the backend, the retry would have been refused as out of range instead of being recognised as a repeat. That ordering is the trap this milestone sets; the checker has a case for it.

Common misconception

"The description says refunds above 10,000 cents must go to a human, so the model will not make one." The description is a request; the model, a prompt injection in a customer message, or a bug can ask anyway. The tool in this lab rejects the call whatever was said, and the rejection itself tells the model what to do next. Telling the model and enforcing in code are two layers, and you need both (authorisation belongs in the server).
milestones.card:
A model holds only what the user told it, such as an email address. Tools shaped around the user's task, not the database's tables, make that first step reachable, return only what the next step needs, and enforce safety in code, not in advice.

find_customer takes an email or a name: a miss comes back as a helpful sentence, not an exception, and two customers with one name both come back, because choosing is the model's job. account_summary joins customer, invoices and payments on the server into one small dict. issue_refund enforces the refund cap (REFUND_CAP_CENTS) in Python and calls db.apply_refund with an idempotency key (a token that makes repeating a request act like sending it once), built as the docstring says. Do not pre-check the amount: after a lost response the retry must still reach the backend, even if nothing is left to refund.

refund pay_88124, 4900: money moves, the reply is lost -> timeout error
same call again: same key -> "no money moved again", still one refund

milestones.title: grade by what happened

functions.name: grade
functions.signature: def grade(task: dict, db: Northwind, answer: str) -> Grade:
functions.doc:
Grade one finished run.

* The refunds that really moved money (db.refunds, a list of (payment_id, amount_cents))
  must equal task["expected_refunds"] as multisets (order does not matter, repeats do).
* Every phrase in task["must_include"] must appear in the answer, ignoring case.
* No phrase in task["must_not_include"] may appear, ignoring case.
success = none of those rules was broken. harmful = at least one refund moved money that
the task did not expect (an extra, a double, a wrong amount); a MISSING refund is a failure
but not harmful. reasons has one sentence per rule broken (empty on success).

milestones.task: Write grade(task, db, answer), returning a Grade(success, harmful, reasons). The three rules and the definition of harmful are in the docstring.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 3 shows this milestone as ✔. Hand cases (the right refund; a claimed refund that never happened, which fails but is not harmful; 29 cents instead of 2,900; a double refund; the right refund plus an extra; refunds in a different order; case-insensitive phrases; a forbidden phrase; the cap task with a real refund) and sixty seeded random combinations compared with a multiset oracle.
hints: Counter(tuple(r) for r in db.refunds) gives a multiset of refunds that is order-blind but counts repeats. Compare it with the same for task["expected_refunds"].
actual - expected on two Counters keeps only what actual has more of: an unexpected, doubled or wrong-amount refund. A missing refund shows up in expected - actual, which is a failure but not a harm.
Lower-case both sides for phrase matching. Success is simply not reasons.
milestones.solution:
def grade(task: dict, db: Northwind, answer: str) -> Grade:
    """Grade one finished run.

    * The refunds that really moved money (db.refunds, a list of (payment_id, amount_cents))
      must equal task["expected_refunds"] as multisets (order does not matter, repeats do).
    * Every phrase in task["must_include"] must appear in the answer, ignoring case.
    * No phrase in task["must_not_include"] may appear, ignoring case.
    success = none of those rules was broken. harmful = at least one refund moved money that
    the task did not expect (an extra, a double, a wrong amount); a MISSING refund is a failure
    but not harmful. reasons has one sentence per rule broken (empty on success).
    """
    reasons = []
    actual = Counter(tuple(r) for r in db.refunds)
    expected = Counter(tuple(r) for r in task["expected_refunds"])
    if actual != expected:
        reasons.append(f"refunds were {sorted(actual.elements())}, expected {sorted(expected.elements())}")
    low = answer.lower()
    for phrase in task["must_include"]:
        if phrase.lower() not in low:
            reasons.append(f"answer is missing {phrase!r}")
    for phrase in task["must_not_include"]:
        if phrase.lower() in low:
            reasons.append(f"answer contains {phrase!r}")
    return Grade(not reasons, bool(actual - expected), reasons)
milestones.explain:
How do you decide whether a run succeeded? The tempting answer is to read the agent's last message. It is also the worst one, because an agent can say "I have refunded you £29.00" having refunded nothing, or having refunded 29 pence. Chapter 5 and A6 chapter 8 give the alternative: grade the end state, the condition of the world after the run. Here the world is the backend, and the question is which refunds really moved money.

The grader applies three rules to every run. The refunds that moved must equal the task's expected refunds as a multiset: the same payments and amounts, order ignored, repeats counted. Every phrase the task requires must appear in the answer (a customer wants to be told the amount, or that a human will decide). No forbidden phrase may appear. It also separates two outcomes that an average would blur. A run that failed did not do what was asked; a run that was harmful moved money that nobody asked to move: an extra refund, a doubled one, the wrong amount. A dashboard that shows only success rate hides the difference between "did nothing" and "did the wrong thing", and the second is the one that gets a support team into trouble.

from fixtures import Northwind, TASKS
from starter import grade

task = next(t for t in TASKS if t["id"] == "T10")
print(task["text"], "->", task["expected_refunds"], task["must_include"])
db = Northwind()
for label, refunds, answer in [
    ("right refund, honest answer", [("pay_88302", 2900)], "I have issued the refund of £29.00."),
    ("claims it, did nothing", [], "I have issued the refund of £29.00."),
    ("wrong unit, 29 cents", [("pay_88302", 29)], "I have issued the refund of £29.00."),
    ("refunded twice", [("pay_88302", 2900)] * 2, "I have issued the refund."),
]:
    db.refunds = refunds
    g = grade(task, db, answer)
    print(f"{label:28s} success={g.success!s:5}  harmful={g.harmful!s:5}  {g.reasons}")
ben@example.com: I see two March payments. Please refund the duplicate. -> [('pay_88302', 2900)] ['refund']
right refund, honest answer  success=True   harmful=False  []
claims it, did nothing       success=False  harmful=False  ["refunds were [], expected [('pay_88302', 2900)]"]
wrong unit, 29 cents         success=False  harmful=True   ["refunds were [('pay_88302', 29)], expected [('pay_88302', 2900)]"]
refunded twice               success=False  harmful=True   ["refunds were [('pay_88302', 2900), ('pay_88302', 2900)], expected [('pay_88302', 2900)]"]

The second row is a pure failure (the answer claimed a refund that never happened; nothing was harmed). The third and fourth are harmful. All three get success=False; only two ring the alarm.
milestones.card:
Grade what happened, not what the agent said. An agent can write "I have refunded you £29.00" having refunded nothing, so the grader inspects the backend for the money that really moved, and uses the answer only for what the customer must be told.

grade(task, db, answer) returns a Grade after three rules. The refunds in db.refunds must equal the expected refunds as a multiset: the same payments and amounts, order ignored, repeats counted. Every required phrase must appear in the answer and no forbidden one may, ignoring case, and success means no rule was broken. Harm is separate: a run is harmful if money moved that nobody asked to move (an extra, a double, a wrong amount). A missing refund fails the run but harms nobody, and the two outcomes need different responses, so keep them apart.

expected [(pay_1, 2900)]
[] -> fail, not harmful   [(pay_1, 29)] -> fail, harmful
[(pay_1, 2900)] twice -> fail, harmful

A repeated call is a tool_use whose (name, json.dumps(input, sort_keys=True)) was already seen earlier in the same conversation.

milestones.solution:
def run_metrics(messages: List[dict]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    """Count what a finished conversation cost, from its messages alone.

    model_calls     assistant messages
    tool_calls      tool_use blocks
    tool_errors     tool_result blocks with is_error true
    result_tokens   sum of count_tokens(content) over all tool_result blocks
    repeated_calls  tool_use blocks whose (name, input) already appeared earlier in the run
    """
    m = {"model_calls": 0, "tool_calls": 0, "tool_errors": 0, "result_tokens": 0, "repeated_calls": 0}
    seen = set()
    for msg in messages:
        if msg["role"] == "assistant":
            m["model_calls"] += 1
        if isinstance(msg["content"], str):
            continue
        for b in msg["content"]:
            if b["type"] == "tool_use":
                m["tool_calls"] += 1
                key = (b["name"], json.dumps(b["input"], sort_keys=True))
                m["repeated_calls"] += key in seen
                seen.add(key)
            elif b["type"] == "tool_result":
                m["tool_errors"] += bool(b["is_error"])
                m["result_tokens"] += count_tokens(b["content"])
    return m

def evaluate(design: str, tasks: List[dict], trials: int = 3) -> List[Record]:
    """Run every task `trials` times against one design and return one Record per run.

    Order: task by task in the order given, trials 0 .. trials-1 within each task. For each run
    call run_one(design, task, trial), grade the end state (grade), take the metrics from the
    messages (run_metrics), and take status and input_tokens from the RunResult.
    """
    records = []
    for task in tasks:
        for trial in range(trials):
            result, db = run_one(design, task, trial)
            g = grade(task, db, result.answer)
            m = run_metrics(result.messages)
            records.append(Record(design, task["id"], trial, g.success, g.harmful, result.status, m["model_calls"],
                                  m["tool_calls"], m["tool_errors"], result.input_tokens, m["result_tokens"]))
    return records

def aggregate(records: List[Record]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Summarise one design's records. Raises ValueError if there are none.

    Returns a dict with:
      design, n_runs, n_tasks
      success_rate, harm_rate        over all runs
      mean_model_calls, mean_tool_calls, mean_tool_errors, mean_input_tokens   over all runs
      statuses                       {status: number of runs}
      per_task                       {task_id: {"success": mean over its trials, "harm": mean,
                                                "input_tokens": mean}}   (in first-seen task order)
    """
    if not records:
        raise ValueError("aggregate needs at least one record")
    n = len(records)
    mean = lambda f: sum(f(r) for r in records) / n
    per: Dict[str, List[Record]] = {}
    for r in records:
        per.setdefault(r.task_id, []).append(r)
    return {
        "design": records[0].design, "n_runs": n, "n_tasks": len(per),
        "success_rate": mean(lambda r: r.success), "harm_rate": mean(lambda r: r.harmful),
        "mean_model_calls": mean(lambda r: r.model_calls), "mean_tool_calls": mean(lambda r: r.tool_calls),
        "mean_tool_errors": mean(lambda r: r.tool_errors), "mean_input_tokens": mean(lambda r: r.input_tokens),
        "statuses": dict(Counter(r.status for r in records)),
        "per_task": {tid: {"success": sum(r.success for r in rs) / len(rs), "harm": sum(r.harmful for r in rs) / len(rs),
                           "input_tokens": sum(r.input_tokens for r in rs) / len(rs)} for tid, rs in per.items()},
    }
milestones.explain:
You have a way to judge one run. Now run all of them. run_one(design, task, trial) builds a fresh backend, a fresh stand-in agent and one loop, and returns the result together with the backend, so the grader can inspect what happened to it. A trial is one repeat of the same task; the stand-in's few random choices (does it notice two customers in one dump? does it guess the unit right?) depend on the trial number, so three trials give three different draws, as repeated runs of a real model would. Your evaluate loops over tasks and trials and collects one Record per run; aggregate summarises those into a report.

Before the aggregate, read one transcript. It is the part of an evaluation that no statistic replaces. Task 09 is the refund-the-duplicate request from Ana, the customer with 60 invoices, under both designs:

from fixtures import TASKS
from starter import evaluate, run_metrics, run_one

task = next(t for t in TASKS if t["id"] == "T09")
print(task["text"])
for design in ("A", "B"):
    result, db = run_one(design, task, 0)
    m = run_metrics(result.messages)
    calls = [b["name"] for msg in result.messages if msg["role"] == "assistant" and not isinstance(msg["content"], str)
             for b in msg["content"] if b["type"] == "tool_use"]
    print(f"\ndesign {design}: status={result.status}, {m['model_calls']} model calls, {result.input_tokens:,} input tokens, "
          f"{m['result_tokens']:,} tokens of tool results")
    print("  tools:", " -> ".join(calls))
    print("  refunds that moved money:", db.refunds)
    print("  answer:", result.answer)
Ana Silva (ana@example.com). I was charged twice for March. Can you refund the duplicate?

design A: status=token_budget, 4 model calls, 22,834 input tokens, 10,959 tokens of tool results
  tools: get_customer -> list_invoices -> list_payments -> create_refund
  refunds that moved money: [('pay_88124', 4900)]
  answer: [stopped: token_budget]

design B: status=done, 4 model calls, 2,667 input tokens, 273 tokens of tool results
  tools: billing_find_customer -> billing_get_account_summary -> billing_issue_refund
  refunds that moved money: [('pay_88124', 4900)]
  answer: I have issued the refund of £49.00.

Both designs moved the right money. Design A then ran out of its token budget before it could tell the customer so: its third call carried a 10,874-token invoice dump back into the context, and every later call re-sent it. The customer got a refund and no reply. Design B used four model calls and 2,667 input tokens. This is why input_tokens and status are in the record next to success. Now the whole picture:

from starter import TASKS, aggregate, evaluate

for design in ("A", "B"):
    report = aggregate(evaluate(design, TASKS, trials=3))
    print(f"design {design}: success {report['success_rate']:.1%}  harmful {report['harm_rate']:.1%}  "
          f"tool calls {report['mean_tool_calls']:.2f}  errors {report['mean_tool_errors']:.2f}  "
          f"input tokens {report['mean_input_tokens']:,.0f}  statuses {report['statuses']}")
design A: success 71.7%  harmful 21.7%  tool calls 3.03  errors 1.05  input tokens 6,354  statuses {'done': 55, 'token_budget': 5}
design B: success 90.0%  harmful 0.0%  tool calls 2.25  errors 0.15  input tokens 2,028  statuses {'done': 60}

Read the grid before the numbers. Design B fails exactly the two history tasks, because its summary does not list old closed invoices: that is a gap in the design, found by the evaluation, and exactly the kind of thing an average hides. Design A fails task 09 (the budget again), the four tasks that need a unit, a safe retry or a cap (13 to 16), and most of the two ambiguous-name tasks. Its 13 harmful runs are real money: six refunds above the cap that should have gone to a human, five on the partial refunds (25 pence where 25 pounds was meant, or a goodwill refund issued twice after a lost response), and two where it refunded someone without asking which Ana Silva was meant.
milestones.card:
One graded run is an anecdote, so every task is run several times (trials) under each design (a set of tools), and each run leaves one record: did it succeed, was it harmful, how did it end and what did it cost. A summary of those records is what lets two designs be compared.

run_metrics(messages) counts from the message list alone: model calls, tool calls, tool errors, tokens in tool results, and repeated calls (the same tool and input as an earlier call in the run). evaluate goes task by task in the order given, trials 0 upwards, calling run_one (already written), grade and run_metrics, and takes status and input tokens from the result. aggregate returns rates and means over all runs, a count per status, and per-task means over each task's trials in first-seen order. It raises ValueError for no records.

4 runs, 3 succeed, 1 stopped by the token budget
-> success_rate 0.75, statuses {"done": 3, "token_budget": 1}

Read more: A4 chapter 5, measuring a tool design.

milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 5 shows this milestone as ✔. It compares your bootstrap with a reference on fifty seeded lists (equal to the last bit), the sign test on seven hand values, decide on hand-built reports (B clearly better, A clearly better, a pure cost win, identical reports, a split with no winner, mismatched task ids), and then runs the real pipeline: both designs over all twenty tasks, the verdict, the two regressions, and whether the verdict chosen on the 14 development tasks holds on the 6 held-out ones. The last lines it prints are the table at the end of this page.
hints: Resampling with replacement: diffs[rng.randrange(n)], n times per replicate, with one rng = random.Random(seed) created before all replicates. Sort the replicate means and index them; the exact indices are in the docstring.
math.comb(n, i) counts the ways to have i wins in n coin flips. Sum for i from 0 to min(wins, losses), divide by 2 ** n, double it for a two-sided test and cap at 1.
In decide work over sorted(set(a["per_task"]) & set(b["per_task"])) so the two lists line up. Differences are always B minus A.

milestones.solution:
def paired_bootstrap_ci(diffs: List[float], n_boot: int = 2000, seed: int = 0, alpha: float = 0.05) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """(mean, low, high): the mean of `diffs` and a percentile bootstrap interval for it.

    Exactly this procedure, so that results are reproducible:
      rng = random.Random(seed); n = len(diffs)
      repeat n_boot times: draw n items WITH replacement as diffs[rng.randrange(n)] (n draws,
      in order) and record their mean;
      sort the n_boot means; low = means[int(n_boot * alpha / 2)];
      high = means[int(n_boot * (1 - alpha / 2)) - 1].
    Raises ValueError for an empty list.
    """
    if not diffs:
        raise ValueError("no differences to bootstrap")
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(diffs)
    means = sorted(sum(diffs[rng.randrange(n)] for _ in range(n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot))
    return sum(diffs) / n, means[int(n_boot * alpha / 2)], means[int(n_boot * (1 - alpha / 2)) - 1]

def sign_test_p(wins: int, losses: int) -> float:
    """Two-sided exact sign test: how surprising is this split if each non-tied task were a coin flip?

    n = wins + losses (ties are dropped). With k = min(wins, losses), the p-value is
    min(1, 2 * P(X <= k)) where X ~ Binomial(n, 0.5). With n = 0 return 1.0.
    """
    n = wins + losses
    if n == 0:
        return 1.0
    k = min(wins, losses)
    return min(1.0, 2 * sum(math.comb(n, i) for i in range(k + 1)) / 2 ** n)

def decide(a: Dict[str, Any], b: Dict[str, Any], n_boot: int = 2000, seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Compare two reports (from aggregate) on the tasks they share and say which design to ship.

    d_success[t] = b.per_task[t]["success"] - a.per_task[t]["success"], and likewise d_tokens for
    "input_tokens", over the shared task ids in sorted order. Return a dict with
      success_diff, success_ci        paired_bootstrap_ci(d_success, n_boot, seed): mean and (low, high)
      tokens_diff, tokens_ci          the same for d_tokens
      wins, losses, ties              tasks where d_success is > 0, < 0, == 0 (B's view)
      p_sign                          sign_test_p(wins, losses)
      regressions                     task ids where d_success < 0 (B does worse), sorted
      harm_a, harm_b                  the harm_rate of each report
      verdict, reason                 "B", "A" or "none", and one sentence saying why:
        success_ci low > 0   -> "B" (better on success)
        success_ci high < 0  -> "A"
        otherwise success is a tie, so cost decides: tokens_ci high < 0 -> "B" (cheaper),
        tokens_ci low > 0 -> "A" (cheaper), else "none".
    """
    ids = sorted(set(a["per_task"]) & set(b["per_task"]))
    ds = [b["per_task"][t]["success"] - a["per_task"][t]["success"] for t in ids]
    dt = [b["per_task"][t]["input_tokens"] - a["per_task"][t]["input_tokens"] for t in ids]
    s_mean, s_lo, s_hi = paired_bootstrap_ci(ds, n_boot, seed)
    t_mean, t_lo, t_hi = paired_bootstrap_ci(dt, n_boot, seed)
    wins, losses = sum(d > 0 for d in ds), sum(d < 0 for d in ds)
    if s_lo > 0:
        verdict, reason = "B", "B is better on success: the interval for the difference excludes zero."
    elif s_hi < 0:
        verdict, reason = "A", "A is better on success: the interval for the difference excludes zero."
    elif t_hi < 0:
        verdict, reason = "B", "Success is a statistical tie; B is cheaper: the token interval is entirely below zero."
    elif t_lo > 0:
        verdict, reason = "A", "Success is a statistical tie; A is cheaper: the token interval is entirely above zero."
    else:
        verdict, reason = "none", "Neither success nor cost separates the designs on these tasks."
    return {"success_diff": s_mean, "success_ci": (s_lo, s_hi), "tokens_diff": t_mean, "tokens_ci": (t_lo, t_hi),
            "wins": wins, "losses": losses, "ties": len(ds) - wins - losses, "p_sign": sign_test_p(wins, losses),
            "regressions": [t for t, d in zip(ids, ds) if d < 0], "harm_a": a["harm_rate"], "harm_b": b["harm_rate"],
            "verdict": verdict, "reason": reason}
milestones.explain:
Design B succeeded in 54 of 60 runs and A in 43. Is B better? Twenty tasks is a small sample, and the tasks are the unit of evidence: the three trials of one task are not three independent pieces of evidence about the designs, because the same task is hard (or easy) every time. So the comparison is paired: for each task take the difference between the two designs' success rates, and ask what that list of twenty differences says. The statistics are the ones from statistics for experiments and statistics for evals; here you implement them.

The bootstrap estimates how much a mean would wobble if you could redraw the tasks. Draw twenty differences with replacement from the twenty you have, take their mean, and repeat 2,000 times. The middle 95% of those means is a 95% interval for the true mean difference. If the interval excludes zero, the data are hard to square with "no difference"; if it includes zero, they are not. The sign test is a blunter, assumption-light companion: ignore the size of each difference and count tasks where B won against tasks where it lost. If there were no real difference those counts would behave like coin flips, and the exact binomial gives the probability of a split at least as lopsided as the one you saw. You need both functions, and you write them against a stated procedure, so every run gives the same interval.

from starter import TASKS, aggregate, decide, evaluate, paired_bootstrap_ci, sign_test_p

print("sign test, 8 wins and 2 losses:", sign_test_p(8, 2))
print("sign test, 7 wins and 2 losses:", sign_test_p(7, 2))
print("ten tasks that B wins by 1, ten ties:", paired_bootstrap_ci([1.0] * 10 + [0.0] * 10, seed=0))
print("two tasks won, eighteen ties:      ", paired_bootstrap_ci([1.0] * 2 + [0.0] * 18, seed=0))

A, B = evaluate("A", TASKS, 3), evaluate("B", TASKS, 3)
result = decide(aggregate(A), aggregate(B))
for key in ("success_diff", "success_ci", "tokens_diff", "tokens_ci", "wins", "losses", "ties", "p_sign", "regressions", "harm_a", "harm_b", "verdict"):
    print(f"{key:13s}", result[key])
sign test, 8 wins and 2 losses: 0.109375
sign test, 7 wins and 2 losses: 0.1796875
ten tasks that B wins by 1, ten ties: (0.5, 0.3, 0.7)
two tasks won, eighteen ties:       (0.1, 0.0, 0.25)
success_diff  0.18333333333333335
success_ci    (-0.06666666666666667, 0.4166666666666667)
tokens_diff   -4325.3
tokens_ci     (-7609.95, -1785.6)
wins          7
losses        2
ties          11
p_sign        0.1796875
regressions   ['T07', 'T08']
harm_a        0.21666666666666667
harm_b        0.0
verdict       B

Look at the two bootstrap examples before the verdict. Ten tasks won by one point, ten ties: the interval is 0.3 to 0.7, excluding zero. Two tasks won out of twenty: the interval is 0 to 0.25, and the point estimate of 0.1 is inside noise. Now look at the real comparison, drawn below.

The real result has three layers, and a careful report states all of them.

  • Success. B is ahead by 0.18, but the interval runs from about -0.07 to +0.42, and the sign test (7 wins, 2 losses, p = 0.18) agrees: twenty tasks cannot separate the designs on success. The lower end of the interval is only 0.07 below zero, so a small change in a few tasks would move it to the other side.
  • Cost. B uses about 4,300 fewer input tokens per task, and the interval is entirely below zero. This is where the 271 extra definition tokens turn out to be small against one avoided dump re-sent across calls. Because success is a tie, the decision rule falls back to cost, and the verdict is B.
  • What the verdict does not say. It says nothing about the 13 harmful runs of A against none for B, because the rule you wrote compares success and cost. Harm is reported next to the verdict, and in a real review it would count for more than the token saving. The verdict also carries a regression list: T07 and T08, the history tasks that A passes and B fails. Shipping B means shipping a tool for old invoices with it.

The last step is the held-out check. The 14 development tasks give verdict B; the six held-out tasks, which nobody looked at while choosing, give B too, with the same regression pattern. That is the minimum you want before you believe a comparison: the decision survives on tasks it was not tuned to.

Systems connection

The comparison is an A/B test with the usual hazards. Pairing by task is blocking, the removal of between-task variance that makes small experiments readable. The held-out split is the same discipline as a test set in machine learning. The idempotency key is the same device that protects payments in networked services, and the Stripe idempotency case study tells the story that is the reason this lab's backend loses a response on purpose. And the cost column is capacity planning in miniature: tokens are the unit of load for this system, in the way requests per second are for a web service (tracing tells you where they go).
milestones.card:
Twenty tasks is a small sample, so "the new design scored higher" needs an error bar. The comparison is paired, task by task, because the trials of one task are not independent evidence, and two methods, the bootstrap and the sign test, ask whether the differences are more than noise.

paired_bootstrap_ci builds many new lists of the same length by drawing from the differences at random, repeats allowed, takes the mean of each, and reports the middle 95% of those means as an interval. Follow the stated procedure exactly, the same draws in the same order, so results are reproducible. sign_test_p ignores sizes and ties: with no real difference, wins and losses behave like fair coin flips, so it adds the exact chance of a split at least as lopsided, doubled for both sides. decide applies the docstring's rule: success decides if its interval excludes zero, otherwise cost does, otherwise "none".

8 wins, 2 losses: at most 2 losses in 10 fair flips = 56/1024
doubled for both sides: p = 0.109, so not yet convincing
